title: Persistent KV cache impact + CUDA graph instability - technical deep dive
summary: Customer wants to understand how Redwood runtime behaves when persistent KV cache is enabled across sessions and how CUDA graphs interact with dynamic kernel selection and eviction. SE showed microbenchmarks highlighting mismatch between graph-captured kernels and runtime kernel routing under quantized models; agreed to run a tailored baseline and share a reproducible benchmark harness and security docs.
transcript:
00:00 Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. We scheduled 45 but plan for 40, is that still good?
00:05 Priya (Aurum): Yep, that's fine. We have Liam and Marcus on for the infra bits. Gwen from security as well.
00:12 Diego (Redwood SE): Quick agenda: reproduce the issue with persistent KV cache, show CUDA graph failure modes we've seen, compare TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM on small and medium seq lengths, and then open Q&A.
00:24 Priya: Perfect. To set context, we're running base Llama2-13B quantized to 4/8 bits on our on-prem cluster (A100s) behind a VPC. Main problem: enabling persistent kv cache for session affinity gives big token savings, but we see sudden latency spikes and occasional OOMs after a few thousand requests.
00:45 Diego: Got it. Two quick clarifying q's: could that be eviction thrash when the KV footprint grows? Or CUDA graph mismatch when graph's assumptions about kernel dispatch don't match when we switch quantized kernels?
00:58 Marcus: We suspected both. The graph instability bit is weird — after a coda graph capture (they pronounced CUDA as coda a few times), the graph sometimes returns slightly higher latency on first few invocations, then drops; other times it keeps spiking every ~200 requests.
01:16 Diego: Right. We see two classes: (A) eviction-induced page-faults or memory compaction when persistent cache grows across sessions, and (B) captured CUDA graphs that pinned a particular kernel ordering; when the runtime later selects a different kernel (e.g., int8-gemm vs fp16-fused), the graph path is invalidated or recompiled which causes latency jitter.
01:40 Liam: What's the difference in behavior between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM here? We run both as experiments.
01:47 Diego: Short answer: TensorRT-LLM tends to prefer precompiled fused kernels and uses Graph capture aggressively; vLLM uses a more dynamic executor that chooses kernels at runtime, so it avoids some graph rewarm costs but may have higher per-token cost.
02:05 Priya: That jives with our observations. With TRT-LLM we see lower steady-state latency but big hiccups. With vLLM it's steadier but costlier.
02:12 Maya: From Redwood's perspective we have kernel selection heuristics that consider sequence-length distribution, KV cache hit rates, and quantization profile. Diego, can you share the microbench you ran?
02:22 Diego: Sure — quick share, I'll paste link after — but in short: baseline harness had 4 workloads: warm (single session, increasing tokens), multi-session persistent KV (affinity pinning), short-seq bursty traffic, and long-trace where evictions happen. We instrumented per-kernel latency and graph compile counts.
02:37 Marcus: When you say "graph compile counts" do you mean CUDA Graph replays vs re-captures?
02:42 Diego: Both. We count how many times we rebuild the graph (capture+compile) vs how many times we just replay a cached graph. Rebuilds are expensive: on A100s they can be hundreds of ms if JIT or driver link happens.
02:55 Priya: Can driver/firmware versions affect this? We're on 525.x drivers.
02:58 Diego: Absolutely, driver and cuDNN/TensorRT minor versions matter — sometimes graph APIs behave differently. We have seen 510 vs 525 differences in graph stability. We'll include a compatibility matrix.
03:10 Gwen (Security): Quick security note: if we're persisting KV cache across sessions, are there any PII risks? We need clarity on encryption at rest and KMS integration.
03:20 Maya: Good call; Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and we can scope a data retention/TTL on persistent caches. We'll add that to next steps.
03:30 Priya: Great. Back to perf: do you have numbers for eviction threshold tuning?
03:33 Diego: Yes. Observed pattern: with a fixed KV capacity per-GPU, once occupancy > ~70% eviction frequency spikes. If eviction policy is LRU naive, you get oscillation: new keys evicted then reinserted causing write amplification. With a size-aware LRU (we call it weighted-LRU) eviction, jitter drops 45% in p99 latency on our microbench.
03:55 Liam: Is that because weighted-LRU prefers keeping longer-lived prefix caches?
03:58 Diego: Exactly — we weight by prefix length and access frequency. That reduces churn.
04:05 Marcus: How do we reproduce the graph instability? Are there synthetic triggers?
04:09 Diego: Yes. Two triggers: (1) flip quantization profile mid-run (e.g., start session with FP16 fused kernels then switch to int8 for new sessions) — graph capture may lock on fp16 kernels and then subsequent int8 kernel selection causes mismatch. (2) dynamic batch size mixing when the graph was captured for a single batch shape.
04:26 Priya: We do dynamic batching in the cluster, so that second one is worrying.
04:29 Diego: For dynamic batches we recommend capture with a set of representative shapes and use multi-shape graph support where available or rely on runtime kernel dispatch for that portion. For TRT-LLM, there's a sweet spot: capture common shapes and fall back to dynamic execution for tails.
04:43 Priya: Can Redwood runtime do that hybrid?
04:45 Diego: Yes — our runtime supports hybrid graph+dispatcher: it will attempt graph replay for shapes in the cache and dispatch for others. If dispatch path changes kernel families, we may re-capture unless we mark graph as "non-recapturable".
04:58 Marcus: Non-recapturable graphs — is that a thing?
05:00 Diego: It's our internal flag to avoid rebuilding costly graphs; but it can cause functional mismatch if kernel assumptions break. We surface this as a metric in the Console: graph_rebuild_count, last_rebuild_reason.
05:12 Liam: Can you show a snippet of the timeline where we saw the OOMs?
05:16 Diego: (screen) Here's a trace: at t=0 warm, t=12k requests p99 ~45ms, at t=14k rebuild happens, memory spikes + 2GB, eviction churn begins, at t=15k we hit OOM because pinned allocations from graph hold.
05:29 Priya: Pinned allocations from graph — is that pinned host or device memory?
05:32 Diego: Device pinned allocations used by TensorRT for workspace. Some graph-recaptures request larger workspaces and the oom comes from those transient allocations plus the persistent KV.
05:43 Priya: So the knobspace is: reduce graph captures, tune eviction policy, limit workspace size, or lower kv persistency?
05:51 Diego: Yes. Also consider limiting per-session KV size or TTL. Another lever is to quantize model differently — int8 often reduces workspace and memory footprint but can change kernel family.
06:04 Marcus: And changing quantization mid-flight is what bites us.
06:08 Diego: Right. We recommend deploying consistent quantization profiles per model version and use model variants rather than switching quantization per session.
06:15 Priya: How would you recommend we benchmark this ourselves?
06:18 Diego: We'll share a harness. Basic plan: 1) Baseline with no persistent KV, grid of batch sizes and seq lengths; 2) enable persistent KV, run long tail (200k requests) with repeated prefixes to exercise hit rates; 3) toggle quantization variant after warm-up and observe rebuild counts; 4) instrument graph_rebuild_count and per-kernel latencies. We'll give you scripts (we have Github gist) that produce perf CSVs.
06:40 Maya: We'll also include a Redwood internal config we used for the run and a recommended config that tuned eviction to weighted-LRU and disabled non-recapturable graphs for the first pass.
06:52 Priya: Can you explain weighted-LRU details? We need to justify it to our infra team.
06:56 Diego: Brief: each KV entry has size and an access frequency counter; eviction score = alpha * size + beta * (1 / freq). We tuned alpha/beta empirically on our workload. Larger prefixes more expensive to evict so score penalizes large size. It's not perfect but reduced churn in tests.
07:17 Liam: What are recommended alpha/beta defaults?
07:20 Diego: Start with alpha=0.7 beta=0.3 for prefix-heavy workloads; alpha down to 0.5 if you see smaller entries being more important. We'll include a tuning doc.
07:30 Gwen: From security/compliance, if we persist KV, we need audit logs of access and TTL enforcement. Can Redwood show per-key access logs?
07:38 Diego: We log per-session key access aggregated by route and user id; we don't ship raw per-token logs by default in hosted, but in Private we can enable detailed audit logging to your SIEM. Also can integrate with KMS for key wrapping.
07:52 Gwen: Good. Also need SOC2 artifact.
07:54 Maya: We'll attach our SOC2 summary and onboarding questionnaire in the follow-up.
08:00 Priya: Back to CUDA Graphs — you mentioned "graph warmup" where first few replays are slower. Why's that?
08:06 Diego: Often because kernels get JIT'ed into the device or the driver's GPU context warms up; memory residency and page table setup can add overhead. Also if the graph calls into kernels that rely on cuBLAS handles that are lazily initialized, the first few calls pay that tax.
08:21 Marcus: So in prod we should run a scheduled warmup after deploy to minimize first-hit jitter?
08:25 Diego: Exactly. Redwood's rollout has an optional post-rollout warmup stage that issues synthetic requests to prime graphs and caches. For sensitive apps we recommend a staged canary warmup.
08:35 Priya: How long should warmup last?
08:37 Diego: Depends: small models a minute; 13B with KV persistent maybe 5-10 minutes of steady traffic. We'll provide heuristics based on model size and mean seq length.
08:47 Liam: If we do warmup, does that avoid the rebuilds entirely?
08:50 Diego: It avoids initial jitter but not rebuilds caused by later kernel-family mismatch or quant profile changes.
08:57 Priya: Do you have direct TRT-LLM vs vLLM numbers on p99 and cost?
09:01 Diego: Quick table I'll paste into chat later, but summary: TRT-LLM with graph capture and aggressive kernel fusion: median ~20-30% lower latency and ~25% lower token cost (due to fewer kernel launches), but p99 can be 2-4x worse if rebuilds happen. vLLM: steadier p99, median higher by ~10-20%. Quantization to int8 can reduce cost further but increases chance of kernel family switches.
09:25 Marcus: Are there any driver flags we should toggle to reduce graph instability?
09:28 Diego: Some; for instance, disabling certain autotune heuristics in cuBLAS can reduce variance. Also enabling persistent kernel caches at driver level helps. We'll include driver-level notes but caution it's infra invasive.
09:43 Priya: For our VPC/on-prem restrictions: can Redwood Private be deployed air-gapped and still get these runtime updates?
09:49 Maya: Yes. Private can operate with offline bundles. We produce controlled runtime releases and patches you can apply. Runtime tuning knobs are in config so no outbound needed.
09:57 Priya: Great. A few nitty-gritty Qs from Marcus: (1) how do you measure per-kernel latency in a quantized fused kernel graph? (2) do you have examples of fallback triggers?
10:06 Diego: (1) We hook into the runtime to emit timestamps before/after kernel launches and aggregate per-kernel signature (op+shape+dtype). For fused kernels we break down by logical op mapping. (2) Fallback triggers: shape mismatch, missing hardware support for certain intrinsics, or when the predicted workspace exceeds available memory. We log fallback_reason along with stack.
10:26 Marcus: Good. We'll need those logs for debugging.
10:29 Diego: We'll enable debug-mode logs for your account for the pilot. Be aware there's an overhead.
10:35 Priya: How about the OOMs — can Redwood detect when graph capture will exceed device memory ahead of time?
10:42 Diego: We have a planner that estimates workspace given kernel policy; but planner errs on the conservative side. When planner predicts an exceed, it chooses a lighter kernel family or disables recapture. We'll share the planner heuristics.
10:55 Liam: What about batching? We do micro-batch coalescing in our router. Should we change that?
10:59 Diego: Coalescing helps throughput but can make graph shapes more variable. For latency sensitive routes, prefer bounded batching (max batch size and max latency window). For throughput, unbounded coalescing ok. We can provide per-route config examples.
11:15 Maya: Recap and next steps — Diego will share benchmark harness, Redwood will propose a recommended config (weighted-LRU, planner conservative), we'll provide driver/compat matrix and SOC2 docs, and schedule a follow-up run where Redwood engineers assist in running the baseline.
11:36 Priya: Timeline? We can do pilot next week.
11:40 Diego: We'll try to get the harness and docs by EOD tomorrow, and be ready to pair next Tue/Thu.
11:48 Priya: Sounds good.
11:50 Gwen: Quick security note — we'll want a short architecture review with your security lead before pilot.
11:55 Maya: We'll schedule that; I'll include Jared from Redwood security.
12:00 Priya: Okay thanks all.
12:03 Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll send notes.
12:05 (call ends)

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mis-typed jargon (coda for CUDA), missing punctuation, some speaker labels are human-assigned and may mismatch. There is light crosstalk and filler words preserved.
